c.text: The **vocal folds** form a vibrating membrane. A **mode** is a pattern of movement across that whole membrane.
children: In **mode 1**, the membrane moves together. In **mode 2**, one region moves up while another moves down. Higher modes divide the surface into more regions moving against one another.
Several modes can occur at the same time. Their movements add together to produce one combined motion.

c.text: The illustrated source has **harmonics**, frequencies at whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency. That lowest frequency is **F0**, the fundamental frequency.
children: A spectrum separates the combined motion into its frequencies. Each spike identifies one contribution; the combined surface does not have to move in just one mode.

c.text: A **fixed–free system** has a fixed end that stays still and a free end that moves. Every allowed mode must fit both conditions.
children: The fixed end is a **node**, a point with no displacement during the cycle. The free end is an **antinode**, where the movement is largest.

c.text: These end conditions allow the **odd harmonics**, at one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency. The second allowed mode is therefore three times the lowest frequency, rather than twice it.
For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end lowers the first mode to half the frequency of the fixed–fixed system.

c.text: A **quarter-wave packet** runs from a node to an antinode. One packet fits the first mode of a fixed–free system because the pattern starts still and ends moving.
Mode 2 fits **three packets** in the same length. Modes 3 and 4 fit five and seven. More packets mean a shorter wavelength and a higher frequency.
children: An even number of packets would finish at a node. That would violate the moving condition at the free end, so the allowed counts are odd.
The packets describe parts of one standing pattern, rather than separate objects traveling along the system.

c.text: The **air in the vocal tract** is a second vibrating system, separate from the vocal folds. Its movement is **longitudinal**, back and forth along the length of the tract.
In the neutral-tube model, the vocal-fold end is **closed** and the lip end is **open**. Air next to the closed end cannot move back and forth there; air at the lips can.
children: The air can be modeled as a chain of masses joined by springs. The mass describes the air that moves, and the spring describes its compression and expansion.

c.text: The air’s resonant frequencies are **formants**. **F1** is the first resonance and **F2** is the second. For a uniform fixed–free tube, their frequencies follow the odd-multiple pattern.
children: The marked locations identify the vowel models: /a/ near one third of the distance from the closed end, /i/ near two thirds, and /u/ at the lips.

c.text: Air can **move back and forth** while neighboring portions stay nearly the same distance apart. That is strong movement with little compression.
Air can also **compress and expand** as neighboring portions approach and separate. This changing spacing supplies the restoring effect called **springiness**.
children: Near the closed end, the air has little movement but strong compression and expansion. At the open end, the air moves strongly with little compression.

c.text: In **mode 1**, motion becomes stronger toward the open end while springiness becomes weaker. Higher modes alternate between regions of strong motion and regions of strong compression more times along the tract.

c.text: At each marked position, ask whether the air mainly **travels together** or **compresses and expands**. The answer comes from the movement throughout the cycle, rather than the air’s position in one still frame.
children: A region where the slices approach and separate strongly is springy. A region where they travel together with little change in spacing mainly shows the moving mass.

c.text: A **constriction** increases both the effective mass and the stiffness of the air. Its effect depends on the mode’s behavior at that location.
children: Where compression is strong and movement is small, the stiffness increase matters more, so the formant rises.
Where movement is strong and compression is small, the mass increase matters more, so the formant falls.

c.text: A **constriction** is a narrowing of the vocal tract. The MRI images show that different vowels place this narrowing in different locations.
children: For **/i/** in dean, the tongue is high and forward, narrowing the tract near two thirds of the distance from the glottis.
For **/u/** in dune, the model emphasizes the narrowing at the lips. For **/a/** in Don, it emphasizes a narrowing farther back, near one third of the distance from the glottis.
The central vowel in done is the neutral comparison, with no marked constriction in this model. Dan has a low, front tongue position.

c.text: The location matters because **each air mode has its own pattern of motion and compression**. The same narrowing can therefore affect F1 and F2 differently.

d.text: The location matters because **each air mode has its own pattern of motion and compression**. The same narrowing can therefore affect F1 and F2 differently.

c.text: Narrowing the tract increases the air’s **effective mass** and **stiffness** at that location. More mass tends to lower a frequency; more stiffness tends to raise it.
The two changes do not automatically cancel. A mode has its greatest movement in different places from its greatest compression.
children: At a strongly moving location, the added mass has the larger effect, so the formant falls.
At a strongly compressing location, the added stiffness has the larger effect, so the formant rises.

c.text: The prediction must be made **for each mode separately**. A location that mainly moves in mode 1 can mainly compress in mode 2, giving opposite changes in F1 and F2.

c.text: Compare **mode 1 and mode 2 at the same location**. Each is a pattern for the whole air column, and each uses that location differently.
children: At the lips, both modes have strong air movement. Inside the tract, one mode can have strong movement where the other has strong compression.
A constriction changes F1 according to mode 1’s behavior there, and changes F2 according to mode 2’s behavior there. F1 and F2 are resonances of the air, separate from the vocal-fold harmonics.

c.text: For **/u/**, narrowing at the lips **loads the free end**. Loading means adding effective mass at the part of the air column that moves strongly.
Both mode 1 and mode 2 have strong movement at the lips, with little compression. The increased mass therefore has the larger effect in both modes, giving **F1 down and F2 down**.
children: The constriction also increases stiffness, but that increase matters little where compression is small.
The low formants in vowels such as dune are consistent with this prediction.

c.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is near **two thirds of the distance from the closed end**. The air behaves differently there in the first two modes.
children: In **mode 1**, the air mainly moves back and forth. The increase in effective mass dominates, so **F1 falls**.
In **mode 2**, the air mainly compresses and expands. The increase in stiffness dominates, so **F2 rises**.

c.text: The resulting /i/ pattern is **low F1 and high F2**. A transition from the neutral vowel into /i/ therefore moves the first formant downward and the second upward.

c.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is farther back, near **one third of the distance from the closed end**.
children: In **mode 1**, strong compression makes the increase in stiffness matter more, so **F1 rises**.
In **mode 2**, strong movement makes the increase in effective mass matter more, so **F2 falls**.

c.text: The first two formants move closer together. This reverses the /i/ pattern, because the constriction is acting at a different location in the two mode patterns.

c.text: **Motion** describes how far a portion of air moves back and forth. **Compression** describes how much the distance between neighboring portions changes.
children: Neighboring portions can move far together and remain evenly spaced. Elsewhere, their individual movement can be small while the distance between them changes strongly.

c.text: The first three modes alternate between these behaviors at different places. To predict a constriction’s effect, follow the relevant mode and check **movement and changing spacing at the constriction**.

c.text: The **vocal-fold source** supplies harmonics. **F0**, its lowest frequency, also sets the spacing between those harmonics.
children: A low F0 puts the harmonics close together. A high F0 places them farther apart.
Greater vocal-fold mass and lower stiffness favor a lower F0. Lower mass and greater stiffness favor a higher F0.

c.text: Changes in **F0 over time** contribute to intonation. The same words, “the dog slept here,” can sound like a statement or a question when their pitch pattern changes.

d.text: Changes in **F0 over time** contribute to intonation. The same words, “the dog slept here,” can sound like a statement or a question when their pitch pattern changes.
children: The pitch change comes from the **vocal-fold source**. The vowel’s formant pattern comes from the **air in the vocal tract**, so changing F0 and changing a formant are different changes.

c.text: The **vocal tract is the filter**. Its resonances, the **formants**, make source harmonics near those frequencies stronger and harmonics farther away weaker.
For the neutral uniform tube, the formants follow the odd-multiple pattern. Constrictions change that pattern.
children: **/u/** has low F1 and low F2. **/i/** has low F1 and high F2. **/a/** has a higher F1 and a lower F2 than the neutral comparison.

c.text: The source supplies the harmonic frequencies, while the filter shapes **their relative strengths**. The resulting spectrum contains both influences.

d.text: The **vocal tract is the filter**. Its resonances, the **formants**, make source harmonics near those frequencies stronger and harmonics farther away weaker.
children: A harmonic near a formant becomes stronger **at its own frequency**. A formant does not move a harmonic onto the formant frequency; it makes nearby available harmonics more prominent.

c.text: The **same vowel filter** can produce different-looking spectra when **F0** changes. F0 determines how many source harmonics fall near the formants.
children: With a low F0, many closely spaced harmonics show the rises and falls of the filter clearly.
With a high F0, the widely spaced harmonics can leave few or no harmonics near a formant. The vowel pattern then becomes harder to identify from the spectrum.

c.text: A spectral slice can be used to identify the source harmonics and measure F0. The lowest harmonic gives the fundamental, and the others occur at its multiples.

c.text: A **spectrum** shows frequency and amplitude at one moment. A **spectrogram** shows how that information changes over time.
children: In a spectrogram, time runs from left to right, frequency runs from low to high, and darker regions indicate greater amplitude.

c.text: The dark formant bands trace the changing vocal tract. During **/ia/**, **F1 rises and F2 falls** as the sound changes from /i/ toward /a/.

children: In a spectrogram, time runs from left to right, frequency runs from low to high, and darker regions indicate greater amplitude.
The **height of a spectral peak becomes darkness** in the spectrogram. A taller peak at one frequency therefore contributes a darker mark at that frequency and moment.

d.text: The dark formant bands trace the changing vocal tract. During **/ia/**, **F1 rises and F2 falls** as the sound changes from /i/ toward /a/.

c.text: Connected speech contains **changing formants**, because the vocal tract changes shape throughout a phrase.
children: In “Where were you a year ago?”, an /i/-like region has low F1 and high F2. The /u/-like sound in you brings the formants down.
The rises and falls of the bands record the changes from one sound to another, rather than a sequence of completely steady vowels.

c.text: A speech-perception experiment joins **the consonant from ma** to **the vowel from na**. Listeners hear **na**, even though the initial consonant was taken from ma.
The vowel contains information about the consonant. The vowel after n has a strong formant transition that differs from the more stationary pattern after m.
children: That transition in the vowel can outweigh the information in the isolated consonant segment.

c.text: **Speech perception uses a stretch of sound over time.** The decision about a consonant can depend on acoustic information in the following vowel.

c.text: A **neural network** can use **F1 and F2** to recognize a vowel. The formants are the input numbers, and the output is a decision about which vowel produced them.
children: **Weights**, often written W, are the numbers that control how the network uses its inputs. Training changes these weights so that the network’s decisions better match the known vowels.

children: **Weights**, often written W, are the numbers that control how the network uses its inputs. Training changes these weights so that the network’s decisions better match the known vowels.

c.text: A **fully connected network** connects every neuron in one layer to every neuron in the next. This one receives two formants, processes them through hidden layers, and has five output neurons.
children: The two inputs are **F1 and F2**. The five outputs represent the vowels in done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.

c.text: Each hidden neuron takes an **inner product**, also called a **weighted sum**. It multiplies each incoming value by its connection weight, then adds the products.
children: This is a **linear network**, with no activation function between layers. Each layer’s results become the next layer’s inputs.

d.text: A **fully connected network** connects every neuron in one layer to every neuron in the next. This one receives two formants, processes them through hidden layers, and has five output neurons.
children: The two inputs are **F1 and F2**. The five outputs represent the vowels in done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.
One pair of formants leads to **one decision among five vowel alternatives**. The output neurons describe competing answers for the same recording, rather than five different recordings.

d.text: Each hidden neuron takes an **inner product**, also called a **weighted sum**. It multiplies each incoming value by its connection weight, then adds the products.
children: This is a **linear network**, with no activation function between layers. Each layer’s results become the next layer’s inputs.

c.text: A **weight** controls how strongly an input contributes to a neuron. For a positive input, a positive weight adds to the next neuron’s value, and a negative weight subtracts from it.
children: The size of the weight controls the size of that contribution. The blue and orange connections distinguish positive and negative weights.

c.text: Before training, the weights are **random**, so they do not yet contain useful knowledge about the vowels. A low F1 and high F2 identify an /i/-like input, but random weights can still lead to the wrong answer.

c.text: In **forward propagation**, the formants pass through the network one layer at a time. Each neuron calculates a weighted sum, and those values become the inputs to the next layer.
The final scores are converted into a **probability distribution** over the five vowels. The probabilities add up to one, and the largest identifies the network’s choice.
children: Here the network favors done even though the input is /i/, as in dean. A valid probability distribution can still give the wrong answer.

c.text: A **target** supplies the known vowel. Training uses the difference between the prediction and the target to change the weights, so a repeated presentation of those formants can favor dean more strongly.

c.text: **PyTorch** provides tools for building a neural network in Python. **nn.Sequential** puts the processing layers in the order that the inputs pass through them.
Each **nn.Linear** specifies the number of inputs and outputs for a weighted-sum layer.
children: The sequence is **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**. The first layer receives F1 and F2; the last produces a score for each of the five vowels.
Each layer’s output size matches the input size of the next layer. Setting **bias=False** removes the bias, an extra constant that would otherwise be added to a weighted sum.

c.text: Declaring this structure **does not train it**. Training also requires examples, their correct answers, and instructions for adjusting the weights.

c.text: A **neural network** takes numbers as input and processes them to make a decision. Here **F1 and F2** describe a vowel, and the network chooses among done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.
children: The input neurons receive the two measurements. The **hidden layers** are the processing layers between the input and output. Each output neuron represents one vowel alternative.

c.text: The network is **fully connected**, so every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer. Each connection has a **weight**, a number that controls its contribution.
children: The weights hold the network’s learned knowledge. Their signs and sizes determine how the incoming values combine in a weighted sum.

d.text: A **neural network** takes numbers as input and processes them to make a decision. Here **F1 and F2** describe a vowel, and the network chooses among done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.
children: The input neurons receive the two measurements. The **hidden layers** are the processing layers between the input and output. Each output neuron represents one vowel alternative.

d.text: The network is **fully connected**, so every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer. Each connection has a **weight**, a number that controls its contribution.
children: The **input values describe one recording**, while the **weights control how recordings are processed**. A new recording changes F1 and F2; learning changes the weights.
The weights hold the network’s learned knowledge. Their signs and sizes determine how the incoming values combine in a weighted sum.

c.text: **Forward propagation** carries the input through the layers to produce an answer. Each neuron calculates an **inner product**, multiplying incoming values by their weights and adding the products.
children: For the marked first-layer neuron, the F1 contribution is positive and the F2 contribution is negative. Their combined effect produces the neuron’s **activation**, its current output value.

c.text: One layer’s activations become the next layer’s inputs. The same weighted-sum operation continues until the output layer has a score for each vowel.
**Softmax** converts the final scores into a **probability distribution**. The probabilities add up to one, and a larger score gives a larger probability.
children: The example gives the highest probability to done, so done is the network’s decision. Making a decision with the learned weights is called **inference**.

d.text: **Forward propagation** carries the input through the layers to produce an answer. Each neuron calculates an **inner product**, multiplying incoming values by their weights and adding the products.
children: For the marked first-layer neuron, the F1 contribution is positive and the F2 contribution is negative. Their combined effect produces the neuron’s **activation**, its current output value.

d.text: One layer’s activations become the next layer’s inputs. The same weighted-sum operation continues until the output layer has a score for each vowel.
**Softmax** converts the final scores into a **probability distribution**. The probabilities add up to one, and a larger score gives a larger probability.
children: **Adding up to one does not make a prediction correct.** Correctness depends on whether the favored vowel matches the vowel that actually produced the recording.
The example gives the highest probability to done, so done is the network’s decision. Making a decision with the learned weights is called **inference**.

c.text: The **computed output** is the network’s prediction. The **desired output**, or **target**, specifies the vowel that actually produced the formants.
children: A **one-hot target** has a one for the correct vowel and zeros for the other vowels. For dean, only the dean position is one.

c.text: The **error**, measured by the **loss**, is the mismatch between prediction and target. The example favors done when the target is dean, so learning should increase the support for dean and reduce the support for the wrong answers.

**Backpropagation** works from the output toward the input to calculate how the error depends on the weights. **Stochastic gradient descent**, or **SGD**, uses that information to make small changes in the weights.
children: The activations from the forward pass are retained for the backward calculation. Repeated weight adjustments gradually improve how the same input is processed.

d.text: The **computed output** is the network’s prediction. The **desired output**, or **target**, specifies the vowel that actually produced the formants.
children: A **one-hot target** has a one for the correct vowel and zeros for the other vowels. For dean, only the dean position is one.
The **target comes from the known recording label**. Learning changes the weights to approach that answer; it does not change the target to agree with the prediction.

c.text: An **activation function** changes a neuron’s weighted sum into the value that it passes on. The **sigmoid** is an S-shaped activation function with outputs between zero and one.
A large negative weighted sum gives an output near zero. A large positive sum gives an output near one.

c.text: **Forward propagation** sends the input through the processing layers. Each neuron calculates an **inner product**, multiplying incoming values by their weights and adding the products.

c.text: The final scores go through **softmax** to become a **probability distribution** over the five vowels. The probabilities add up to one; the largest gives the network’s choice.

c.text: The vowel plot places **F1 on the horizontal axis** and **F2 on the vertical axis**. Each point is one recording, and its color identifies the vowel.
Each category forms a **cloud of points** because speakers and recordings vary. Dean tends toward low F1 and high F2, while Dan extends toward higher F1.

c.text: A **vector** is a list of numbers. The vowel network takes one **static vector**, one pair of F1 and F2 measurements, and decides among a few categories.
In **parallel distributed processing**, neurons within a layer calculate responses in parallel, and information is spread across many neurons.
children: The weights determine how the numbers are processed. Backpropagation supports learning by relating errors to those weights.

The early **McCulloch and Pitts** model used the all-or-none character of neural activity. The **Parallel Distributed Processing** approach developed networks in which many neurons process and represent information together.

c.text: Speech and language also involve **sequences**. Formants change over time, and words arrive in an order. Modeling those patterns requires using information across moments, rather than only one fixed input vector.

c.text: A **recurrent neural network** uses **feedback**: output from one moment returns through state units and affects processing at the next moment. This allows the current response to depend on recent history.
In **Jordan’s network**, plan units specify the sequence to produce, hidden units combine information, output units produce the response, and state units carry information from recent outputs.
children: The plan and state information both feed the hidden layer. The output then updates the state, keeping the sequence going.

c.text: The speech-production traces show that articulatory features can extend across several sounds. Rounding, for example, can rise early and stay active through part of the sequence.

c.text: A **single neuron** takes an input vector and returns one weighted sum. A **neural network** connects many neurons so that one input vector produces an output vector, such as scores for five vowels.
A **large language model**, or **LLM**, takes a sequence of vectors and predicts the next item. Each vector is a list of numbers representing an item such as a word.
children: The **context window** is the available sequence used for the prediction. Fifteen input vectors and a sixteenth-item prediction are a small example, rather than a fixed limit on the idea.
Layers of learned weights transform the input representations until the model produces probabilities for the next item.

c.text: For **learning**, an existing sequence supplies the correct continuation. Predicting the next word and comparing that prediction with the real word gives an error for backpropagation and **SGD** to use.
An **agentic system** connects whole LLMs with different jobs. One produces an outline, another writes a draft, a critic checks it, and a reviser changes it.
children: The critic and reviser can form a loop before the final answer is produced. **Hallucination** means producing invented information; criticism and revision aim to detect and reduce it.

c.text: **Inference** uses learned weights to produce an answer. **Learning** changes those weights through error-based adjustments. The prediction task requires useful knowledge about how the available information can be completed.
**Gestalt completion** uses the structure already present to supply missing information. The next-item task trains a system to supply a missing continuation from the available sequence.

**Gestalt completion** uses the structure already present to supply missing information. The next-item task trains a system to supply a missing continuation from the available sequence.

c.text: A model can use **fifteen vectors to predict the sixteenth**. The important operation is predicting the next item from the available sequence; the vectors can represent several kinds of material.

For **words**, the sentence so far supplies the context. In “The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the …”, predicting a continuation requires tracking that the cat is the one that sat.

For **sound**, consecutive spectrogram frames become vectors. Predicting the next frame uses the sound over time. For **pictures**, patches are put in row-by-row order so the model can predict a missing patch.
For a **protein**, the sequence consists of amino acids. The insulin example leaves the next amino acid to be predicted.
children: Words, sound frames, picture patches and amino acids reach the model as lists of numbers. The material differs, but the next-item task remains the same.

c.text: **Phonotactic knowledge** is knowledge of which sound sequences a language allows. English permits a simple **consonant–vowel–consonant** syllable in words such as mat, cup and dog.
children: The pattern concerns sounds. Two letters can spell one consonant sound, as in ship, and a silent letter does not add a sound.

c.text: An **onset** is the consonant or consonant group before a syllable’s vowel. A **coda** is the consonant or consonant group after it.
children: English allows some consonant orders and excludes others. Flat is possible, but the starred lfat is not. Help is possible, but hepl is not. A star marks an impossible English form.

c.text: A word can contain several syllables, so a sequence must also be checked against the **syllable boundaries**. The t and l can occur across the boundary in At-lan-tic, although tl cannot start an English syllable.
children: The ng sound can end a syllable, as in ring, but it cannot begin one in English.

c.text: **Next-letter prediction** reveals knowledge of possible English sequences. Some beginnings allow many continuations, while others sharply restrict the next letter.
After **ra**, many letters are possible because the vowel has already arrived. After **skr**, a vowel is expected. After **sp**, l, r or a vowel can follow, while n is excluded in this onset pattern.
children: The predictions follow spelling as well as sound. After k, n is possible in a word such as knee, even though the k is silent.

c.text: A **probability distribution** can express these expectations. Many plausible continuations produce a broad distribution; strong constraints concentrate probability on a few choices.
children: Learning to predict the next letter requires learning the sound and spelling patterns that make those predictions accurate.

c.text: A **neuron** receives a vector, a list of input numbers, and calculates one **weighted sum**. A **neural network** combines many neurons and returns an output vector with a score for each possible answer.

A **large language model** processes a sequence of vectors to predict the next item. Its layers change the numerical representation of the sequence, ending in a distribution over possible continuations.

An **agentic system** connects whole language models. The outline, writing, criticism, revision and final-answer stages are different jobs, and the critic and reviser can exchange a draft more than once.
children: The models communicate through messages in human or computer languages.

c.text: **Inference** produces an answer using learned weights. **Learning** compares predictions with targets and adjusts those weights, using SGD and the backward calculation organized through dynamic programming.

c.text: A **representation** is the information about an item carried in its vector. An LLM changes these representations through many layers to make a useful next-item prediction.
Several **heads** work in parallel within a layer. Each is a processing component with learned weights that contributes information, and the layer brings their contributions together.
Successive layers use the representations produced by the layer before them. The result of one stage becomes the input for another, allowing the information to develop through the model.

children: A head is a component **inside one language model**. An agent in the outline-and-revision system is a **whole language model** assigned a job.

d.text: Successive layers use the representations produced by the layer before them. The result of one stage becomes the input for another, allowing the information to develop through the model.
children: **More heads** means more parallel contributions within a layer. **More layers** means more successive stages of processing. These describe the model’s width and depth, respectively.

c.text: A **dynamical system** applies a rule to its current state to produce a new state, then uses that updated state again. Its **trajectory** is the sequence of states that results.
children: For an oscillator, position and velocity are the changing state values. Repeated updates produce its back-and-forth movement.

c.text: A **recurrent network** carries its recent output back through state units as processing continues over time. The same learned connections are used at each time step.
In an **LLM**, the vectors change as they pass through successive layers. Depth supplies the sequence of changes: each layer uses the values produced by the preceding layer.
children: The layers have their own sets of weights. Following a value through them gives a changing path, but that path does not have to be an oscillator’s repeating curve.

c.text: The stock-return paths show different values developing along different trajectories. A trajectory describes how a quantity changes across the ordered stages being followed.

For a **protein**, amino acids supply the sequence. The next item in the illustrated insulin sequence is **Y**.

c.text: Predicting the **next letter** depends on the sequence already present. Some beginnings allow many completions, while others permit only a few.
After **ra**, several consonants can follow. After **skr**, the next letter is a vowel. After **sp**, l, r or a vowel can follow, while n is excluded from that onset pattern.
children: Spelling also matters. After k, n can occur in knee, although that k does not represent a spoken sound.

c.text: The prediction can be expressed as a **probability distribution** over letters. A broad distribution allows many continuations; a concentrated one gives most of its probability to the few continuations that fit.
children: The model can improve only by learning regularities in the words it is trying to continue. Accurate next-letter prediction therefore reveals knowledge of English sound and spelling patterns.

Repeated **prediction and correction** can put these constraints into the weights. The training task asks for a continuation, even though succeeding at it requires knowledge about the structure of words.

c.text: A **character-level transformer** is an LLM trained to predict the next character, or letter. Existing words supply both the sequence so far and the correct next letter.
children: Training compares the prediction with the true continuation and adjusts the weights. Better predictions require learning which sound and spelling sequences English permits.

c.text: The small model has **four heads in each of five layers**, with **64 numbers in each token vector**. A token is an input item represented by a vector, and the vector’s **dimension** is its number of values.
children: The heads contribute within each layer. The layers transform the representations through successive processing stages.

c.text: Generated word examples reveal the model’s current knowledge. Early outputs can be poorly formed; more training and more words can help the output reflect English syllable patterns.
